Welcome—I'm glad you're here.
Imagine wandering through the shadowed streets of Victorian London, where the lives of five remarkable women, Polly, Annie, Elizabeth, Catherine, and Mary Jane, quietly unfolded.
Their paths crossed with a figure whose name has echoed through history—Jack the Ripper. But what if, together, we could finally turn the spotlight away from the legend and onto the women themselves?
That’s exactly what Hallie Rubenhold sets out to do in The Five: The Untold Lives of the Women Killed by Jack the Ripper. She invites us to discover the overlooked humanity, struggles, and resilience behind each name—a chance to see these women not as mere victims, but as individuals navigating the relentless challenges of poverty, prejudice, and a world stacked against them.
As we walk alongside them, we’ll uncover stories of dreams, disappointments, and daily battles for dignity—a side of history so often neglected. These aren’t just five tragic tales. They’re windows into the heart of Victorian England’s overlooked underbelly, where survival was a feat and hope was hard-won.
Together, we’ll explore what happens when we reclaim voices lost to time. We’ll ask ourselves: what do we learn, not just about the women, but about the world that let them slip through the cracks?
So, let’s embark on this journey—not to chase the shadow of a killer, but to rediscover the light and strength of those who deserve to be remembered.

Chapter 1: Shifting the Spotlight from the Killer to the Women
When most folks think of Victorian London’s darkest corners, their minds jump right to a name that sends a chill down the spine: Jack the Ripper. For over a century, people have obsessed over the mystery of who he really was, the grisly details of his crimes, and the foggy streets where he lurked.
But—let’s pause for a moment. Beneath all those headlines and the myths, there were five women whose lives have nearly disappeared from our memories. Their names—Mary Ann Nichols, Annie Chapman, Elizabeth Stride, Catherine Eddowes, and Mary Jane Kelly—are usually just footnotes, buried under the weight of the Ripper’s legend.
This story? It’s not about the man who killed them. It’s about the women themselves. Women who lived, struggled, and held onto hope in a world that barely gave them a voice.
Now, when most people hear about these women, they picture a tired stereotype: the so-called fallen woman, the prostitute, the inevitable victim. But honestly, the truth is so much deeper—and far more human. Each one of these women was born into a world with strict rules about what a woman could be, especially if she was poor.
Their lives were shaped by the everyday grind of class, gender, and circumstance. They were daughters, wives, mothers, workers, and wanderers. They laughed, they loved, they lost. They made choices—sometimes hopeful, sometimes desperate—because that’s all the world allowed.
Picture London in the late 1800s. It’s a city of sharp contrasts—booming, bustling, and bursting at the seams. The wealthy had their grand houses and glittering parties, while the poor squeezed into cramped rooms, faced hunger, and lived with the constant threat of being cast aside. The East End, where these women lived and died, was a maze of overcrowded lodging houses, noisy factories, and smoky pubs. It was a place where your luck could change overnight—or vanish just as quickly.
In this world, women like Mary Ann, Annie, Elizabeth, Catherine, and Mary Jane were almost invisible. Their struggles weren’t unique, but their stories rarely got told. Instead, they’ve been defined by the violence that ended their lives, their identities flattened into a single, dismissive label. But if you look closer, you’ll see something remarkable: resilience, resourcefulness, and a stubborn refusal to give up—even when the odds were stacked against them.
It’s easy to forget these women were once children, growing up in families who dreamed of better futures. Some were born into more comfort, others into hardship. Some learned to read and write, while others never had that chance. As they grew up, they faced the same challenges as so many women of their day—finding work, keeping a roof overhead, caring for children, and trying to navigate a society that judged them harshly for every misstep.
The story of the Five isn’t just about how their lives ended. It’s about how they lived—the choices they made, the people they loved, the dreams they chased, and the hurdles they faced. It’s about how society failed them, and how history has all but forgotten them.
When you shift the focus away from the man who killed them and really look at the women themselves, a whole new picture appears. It’s richer, more complicated, and, above all, more human.
As you listen to their stories, you’ll see that the true tragedy isn’t just the violence they suffered, but the way their humanity has been erased by the myths that followed. Most people don’t realize how easily a person’s story can disappear when the world decides they don’t matter anymore. But in the details of their lives—the work they did, the families they cared for, the struggles they endured—you’ll find something that simply can’t be erased: the stubborn dignity of ordinary people trying to survive in a world that gave them almost nothing to work with.

Chapter 2: Mary Ann Nichols and the Weight of Poverty
Picture a young girl in the heart of London, growing up in a world where every single penny mattered. That’s Mary Ann Nichols—her friends called her Polly. Her father worked as a locksmith, and while it was steady work, it didn’t exactly bring comfort or security. The family squeezed into tight quarters, sharing space with neighbors and relatives, always knowing that just one bit of bad luck could send them spiraling into poverty.
Polly learned the hard way that life’s a constant balancing act. School? That was just a short chapter—most kids in her neighborhood were out working as soon as they could, doing whatever it took to help their families get by.
Like many women of her time, Polly married young, hoping for a little stability, maybe even a place she could truly call home. She and her husband William had five kids together. For a while, it looked like things might just work out. But poverty has a way of wearing people down, doesn’t it? The pressure never really lets up, and before long, cracks started to show.
William’s job as a printer’s machinist was steady, but those wages barely covered the basics. Then, when Polly’s mother passed away, the family lost a crucial source of support. Home life got tense—money was always tight, and the daily grind just made things worse. Eventually, their marriage couldn’t take it anymore. Polly left, and with that choice, she lost more than her husband. In Victorian England, a woman who walked away from her marriage often lost her children, her family, and any shot at respectability.
After that, Polly drifted from one workhouse to another, spending nights in lodging houses that got rougher each time. The workhouse was the last stop for people with nowhere else to turn. Conditions were harsh, the rules were strict, and the shame was heavy. Most folks ended up there because they simply had no other options.
Polly did her best to find work as a domestic servant, but jobs were scarce and competition was fierce. Employers wanted spotless reputations, and Polly’s past always seemed to follow her around.
Sometimes, she scraped together just enough money for a bed in a cheap lodging house. These places were crowded and noisy—people living right on the edge. Nights were filled with the sounds of coughing, arguing, and, every now and then, a burst of laughter. Come morning, everyone scattered, each hoping to find work or a little charity—just enough for another night indoors.
The tough part is, Polly’s story wasn’t unique. So many women faced that same exhausting cycle: a little hope, then disappointment. London was full of people like her—women who once had families, homes, even dreams, now just scraping by. The streets of Whitechapel were especially unforgiving for women alone. There was always the threat of violence, always the fear of having nowhere left to turn.
But you know what? Polly kept going. She found small moments of kindness—a friend who’d share a meal, a stranger who’d give a few coins. She did her best to stay hopeful, even as the world seemed to close in around her.
In the end, surviving in Victorian London took more than money—it took real resilience. It’s easy to overlook the quiet strength it takes to keep moving forward when everything’s stacked against you.
When Polly’s life ended in a dark corner of Whitechapel, the newspapers were quick to slap a label on her, to reduce her to just one word. But her story is so much more than that. She was a mother, a daughter, a woman who kept trying to make the best of what she had. Her life was shaped by poverty, by class, by the expectations placed on women—but she never stopped searching for a way through.
And when we remember Polly, we get the chance to see the humanity that’s so often lost in stories like hers.

Chapter 3: Annie Chapman and the Fragility of Respectability
Let’s step back into the bustling streets of Victorian London, where respectability wasn’t just a social status—it was a lifeline, especially for women.
Annie Chapman’s life shows us just how quickly everything could change, and how tough it was to hold on to even the smallest bit of security.
Annie was born into a family that managed, for a while, to keep things afloat. Her father worked as a coachman, which meant a modest but steady paycheck. Annie’s childhood had its ups and downs, sure, but there was always dinner on the table and a roof overhead. She even learned to read and write—something that set her apart from a lot of other kids back then.
As Annie grew up, she married John Chapman, who was also a coachman, just like her dad. Together, they carved out a life that, by the standards of their time, was comfortable. They had three kids, and for a little while, things felt stable. But life can be unpredictable, can’t it?
Their oldest daughter was born with a disability, and caring for her stretched the family’s resources to the limit. Then tragedy struck—their only son died of meningitis. That loss was something Annie and John never really recovered from.
Grief and hardship started to take their toll. Both Annie and John turned to drinking, trying to numb the pain in a world that offered so few comforts. John ended up losing his job, and suddenly, their finances fell apart. Eventually, their marriage broke down, and Annie was left on her own, separated from her children and everything she’d known.
In Victorian society, a woman without a husband or family wasn’t just alone—she was vulnerable. Once respectability slipped away, it was almost impossible to get it back.
Annie drifted from one lodging house to another, scraping by however she could. She took whatever work she could find—cleaning, sewing, selling flowers on the street—but steady jobs were few and far between. The streets of Whitechapel were crowded with women just like her, each one doing their best to hold onto a shred of dignity in a world that didn’t give much back.
Still, Annie tried to keep up appearances. She was known for her neatness, her tidy hair, and her polite manners. Even when money was tight, she made an effort to look presentable. It was her way of pushing back—a small but powerful act of defiance against the odds stacked against her.
Annie’s story really highlights how the line between respectability and ruin was razor-thin. Most folks don’t realize just how fast a life can unravel—how one tragedy, a lost job, or a broken marriage could send someone from comfort to desperation almost overnight. And for women like Annie, the safety net was full of holes. There just weren’t many resources or second chances if you slipped through.
When Annie’s life ended, the newspapers didn’t waste any time judging her. They called her a woman of the streets, completely erasing the years she spent as a wife and mother, the hardships she faced, and the dignity she fought to maintain. But Annie’s story isn’t about failure—it’s about resilience.
If we really remember Annie, it’s clear that respectability isn’t just about how someone looks on the outside. It’s about the quiet strength it takes to keep going, even when the world turns its back.

Chapter 4: Elizabeth Stride and the Search for Belonging
In the swirl of London’s immigrant neighborhoods, searching for a sense of belonging was almost a daily battle. Elizabeth Stride’s story is really shaped by movement—crossing borders, jumping between social classes, and pushing against what society thought a woman should be.
Elizabeth was born in Sweden, the daughter of a farming family, where life meant hard work and simple living. Like so many young women in rural Europe back then, she left home chasing the promise of something better, and eventually landed in the lively city of Gothenburg. There, she found work as a domestic servant. It gave her a bit of freedom, sure, but not much in the way of security.
Then, life took an unexpected turn. Elizabeth became pregnant, but heartbreakingly, the child didn’t survive. In a society that judged women harshly for stepping out of line, her choices became painfully limited. So, she moved to London, joining the wave of immigrants hoping for a fresh start on the city’s crowded streets.
London was full of both promise and peril. If you were new, the city could welcome you—or turn cold in an instant. Elizabeth married a carpenter named John Stride, and together they opened a coffee house in the East End. For a moment, it looked like things might work out. The business brought them purpose, a place in the community, and a glimmer of stability.
But running a small business in a tough neighborhood was no easy feat. The coffee house struggled, and soon, so did their marriage. Elizabeth and John separated, and once again, she found herself on her own. She moved through a string of lodging houses, picking up whatever work she could—cleaning, sewing, selling flowers, sometimes leaning on charity just to get by.
Even with all these struggles, Elizabeth was known for her warmth and her willingness to help others. She’d look after sick friends, share whatever little she had, and tried hard to keep some sense of community alive, no matter how tough things got. People in the neighborhood knew her—she was someone who always tried to make the best of a hard situation.
You know, Elizabeth’s story really shows how powerful the search for belonging can be. Most folks don’t realize just how much it matters to feel like you’re part of something—to have your own place, some purpose, and people who care. For immigrants and outsiders, that struggle to fit in can feel overwhelming. The city held out opportunities, but it demanded resilience and a willingness to adapt.
When Elizabeth’s life came to a tragic end, the newspapers mostly focused on her outsider status—a woman on the margins. They missed the years she spent trying to build a life, the kindness she showed, and the quiet determination that kept her moving forward. Remembering Elizabeth reminds us that belonging isn’t just about where you come from. It’s about the connections you create, and the ways you care for the people around you.

Catherine Eddowes and the Cost of Independence
Let’s dive into the story of Catherine Eddowes—a woman who, in a world with so few options for women, still managed to carve her own path. Catherine wasn’t someone who let others decide who she was supposed to be. Her life? It was a patchwork of adventures, setbacks, and those small but meaningful victories that show just how powerful resilience can be.
Catherine’s journey started in Wolverhampton, where her father worked with tinplate. When she was just a child, her family packed up and moved to London, hoping for something better. But life, as it often does, threw her a curveball—she lost both parents while she was still young. Suddenly, Catherine and her siblings were left to figure things out on their own, and she ended up in a workhouse. It was shelter, sure, but comfort? Not so much.
As she got older, Catherine just couldn’t accept the idea that her circumstances would define her. She left the workhouse behind and headed to Birmingham, where she found a job in a factory. That’s where she met Thomas Conway. With him, Catherine hit the road—they worked as hawkers, selling wares on the street, and even performed for crowds. She built a reputation for her quick wit, her love of music, and how easily she made friends wherever she went.
Life on the road was unpredictable. But for Catherine, it offered something rare—a sense of freedom most women back then could only dream about. She and Thomas had three children, and for a while, they managed to get by. Still, the pressure of living on the edge, the struggle to raise a family, and the temptations that came with hardship started to wear them down. Eventually, their relationship fell apart, and Catherine was left to make it on her own again.
She moved back to London, where she met John Kelly, a laborer who became her new partner. The two of them scraped by, moving from one cheap lodging house to another, picking up whatever work they could. Catherine was nothing if not resourceful—she sold little trinkets, cleaned houses, and just did what she had to in order to survive. People knew her for her sense of humor, her generosity, and most of all, her stubborn refusal to give up.
Here’s something to pay attention to: independence always comes with a price. Most folks don’t see the sacrifices that go into making your own way—the risks you take, the loneliness, the never-ending hustle. For women like Catherine, the world was stacked against them, but she never stopped pushing forward.
When Catherine’s life ended, newspapers focused on the circumstances of her death, barely mentioning the years she spent fighting for something better. They missed the courage it took to get back up every time she was knocked down, the creativity she poured into every challenge, and the warmth she shared with the people around her.
So, here’s the real takeaway: independence isn’t just about standing alone. It’s about finding ways to survive—and even thrive—when the odds are against you. That’s the spirit Catherine Eddowes brought to every chapter of her life.

Chapter 6: Mary Jane Kelly and the Dream of Escape.
Have you ever felt that deep ache—the one that comes from wanting to start over? To just walk away from the weight of old mistakes, and from the way people seem to look right through you, never seeing who you really are? For Mary Jane Kelly, the youngest of the Five, that longing for a fresh start wasn’t just a passing thought—it was the thread running through every part of her short, stormy life.
Mary Jane’s story can be tough to piece together. She was a woman who wore many names, whose history flickers between rumor and truth. What we do know is that she was born in Ireland, probably into a family always scrambling to get by. Like so many, her family was swept along by the tide of migration, landing in Wales, hoping for work and a steadier life. The world Mary Jane stepped into was full of uncertainty—each day brought its own hurdles, and the future was always a question mark.
As a teenager, she ended up in London—a city that promised so much, but rarely delivered on its promises, especially for women like her. She worked as a domestic servant, a laundress, and, sometimes, as a sex worker. The line between getting by and being judged was razor-thin, and Mary Jane often found herself on the wrong side of it. But she wasn’t just another hard-luck story. She was known for her charm, her quick wit, and her knack for starting over. She’d spin tales about Paris, about wealthy admirers and grand adventures. Did it matter if those stories were true? Not really—they were her way of picturing a life bigger than Whitechapel’s narrow, gray streets.
All Mary Jane really wanted was something simple: a place of her own. Just a small room, a door she could close to the world. For a little while, she had it—a tiny space in Miller’s Court, a place she could actually call home. She decorated it with cheap prints and bits of lace, trying to carve out a bit of beauty in the middle of all the hardship. Friends remembered hearing her sing old Irish ballads late into the night, her voice drifting through the thin walls, reaching out for something better.
But London wasn’t kind. Mary Jane’s grip on safety was always slipping. She took in lovers, opened her door to friends, and shared what little she had, always trying to keep hope alive. There were bright moments—nights filled with laughter, mornings when sunlight made everything seem possible. But there were also long stretches of loneliness, fear, and hunger.
When her life ended, the newspapers jumped at the drama, turning her story into headlines about violence and mystery. But they missed something important—the quiet courage it takes to keep dreaming, even when everything is stacked against you. Most people don’t realize just how powerful the hope of escape can be, or how much strength it takes to keep reaching for a better life, even when the world keeps shutting the door.
So, when we think of Mary Jane Kelly, let’s remember this: the dream of escape isn’t just about running away. It’s about holding on to the stubborn belief that life can be different, that even the most battered heart can find a place to rest.

Chapter 7: The World They Inherited—Victorian Society’s Cage.
Have you ever wondered why those women’s lives seemed so unbelievably tough, or why their choices felt so limited? Well, the truth is, the world they stepped into was stacked against them from the very beginning. The rules were strict, and for women without family or money to back them up, there just wasn’t much room for mistakes.
Victorian London—now that was a city of contradictions. On one hand, you had new inventions popping up, industries growing fast, and this exciting promise of a better life. But at the same time, there was heartbreaking poverty, slums packed tighter than you can imagine, and a social ladder so rigid most folks never climbed a single rung. And for women? The expectations were even tighter. Respectability wasn’t just important—it was everything. One wrong move could lead to social disaster.
The Five lived in a world where finding work was tough, and the jobs they could get—like working as a laundress, cleaning houses, or sewing—barely paid enough to keep the hunger away. Marriage was supposed to offer safety, but honestly, it was a gamble. If your husband died, or things fell apart, or even just one rumor started about you, it could mean total ruin.
Think about the safety nets we have today—public assistance, shelters, social services—back then, those were either missing completely or so limited they didn’t help much. The workhouse was the last stop, and it carried a heavy sense of shame. Most people would rather take their chances on the street than face that kind of humiliation.
And then, there was the ever-present threat of violence. Walking alone at night in Whitechapel was genuinely dangerous, especially for women. The police? More often than not, they didn’t seem to care. The newspapers loved to make the East End sound like a pit of sin and crime, which only made things worse for the people trying to get by there.
But even in this harsh world, you’d still find moments of real kindness. Neighbors shared what little they had—food, coins, even just a warm place to sit. Women leaned on each other, forming quiet networks to find jobs or a bed for the night. It turns out, surviving wasn’t just about grit—it was about community and looking out for one another.
Most of us don’t realize just how much the world around us shapes our options, or how easy it is to judge when we’re looking in from the outside. The Five weren’t just the victims of one brutal man—they were survivors of a society that offered them almost no chances, and even less compassion.

Chapter 8: The Aftermath—How the Five Were Remembered
After those terrible murders, the whole city felt caught between fear and fascination. Newspapers ran wild with sensational headlines, spinning out theory after theory about who the killer might be. But you know what’s heartbreaking? The women themselves were barely ever the focus. They were painted with broad strokes—just “unfortunates” or “fallen women”—their real lives quickly overshadowed by the gruesome story.
In the weeks that followed, the police did their best, but the investigation kept hitting walls: prejudice, mistakes, and just not enough resources. Everyone was obsessed with finding the killer, rarely stopping to think about the lives that had been lost. Those five women—Mary Ann, Annie, Elizabeth, Catherine, and Mary Jane—became more like symbols than real people, their true stories hidden beneath layers of rumor and myth.
For the families and friends left behind, the loss was crushing. Imagine children suddenly without their mothers, siblings missing their sisters, or friends left with empty spaces in their lives. The local community genuinely grieved, but the rest of the world seemed to move on. Slowly, the names of the Five faded away, replaced by the shadowy legend of Jack the Ripper.
As years went by, the murders turned into a kind of dark entertainment. Books, movies, even guided tours—people got caught up in the mystery and the horror. The women at the center of it all? They were barely mentioned, except as victims. Their dreams, their challenges, their kindness—those parts of their stories just disappeared.
Still, there were always some who remembered. In quiet corners of the neighborhood, neighbors would talk about Mary Ann’s kindness, Annie’s determination, Elizabeth’s generosity, Catherine’s sense of humor, and Mary Jane’s hope for a better future. These whispered memories, shared between families and friends, kept their spirit alive in ways the headlines never could.
It really shows how the way we remember the past shapes the present, doesn’t it? Most of us don’t realize just how quickly a person’s story can be erased, or how powerful it is to reclaim the voices of those who’ve been silenced. That’s something worth remembering.

Chapter 9: Reclaiming Their Stories—A New Kind of Remembrance
Over the past few years, there’s been this powerful movement—a shift that’s taken the spotlight off the killer and shined it right where it belongs: on the women themselves.
Historians, writers, and activists have been working hard to uncover who the Five really were. They’re piecing together lives from scraps of evidence and faded memories, determined to tell the real stories.
But you know, it’s about so much more than just correcting the record. It’s about honoring the dignity, the strength, and the resilience of women who’ve been overlooked for far too long.
When we share their stories, we challenge the old stereotypes that have defined them for over a century. Suddenly, we’re not just seeing victims—we’re meeting individuals. Women with dreams, with fears, with hopes that mattered.
Reclaiming their stories isn’t easy. The records are spotty, and time has erased so much. But here’s the thing—every single detail counts. Whether it’s a letter, a census entry, or a memory passed down through a family, each fragment helps build a fuller, richer picture of who these women truly were.
And as more of their stories come into the light, something interesting happens. The legend of Jack the Ripper starts to fade into the background, and the women themselves finally step forward. Their lives become a lens—a way for us to understand not just their world, but also how society let them down.
Most people don’t realize just how much history is shaped by those who tell it. By reclaiming the stories of the Five, we’re making space for other forgotten voices, too. And we’re reminding ourselves that, in the end, every life truly matters.

Chapter 10: The Legacy of the Five—Lessons for Today
When you stand at the edge of history, it's easy to imagine that the world of the Five is far behind us. Their struggles might feel like they belong to another time entirely. But if you listen closely, you’ll still hear the echoes of their lives—especially in the stories of women today who are facing poverty, homelessness, violence, and the heavy weight of judgment.
The lessons the Five left behind? They aren’t just history. They’re alive in our present, and they can shape our future too. They remind us that everyone—no matter where they come from—has a story worth hearing. Dignity isn’t just for the lucky few, and resilience? It often shows up in places you’d never expect.
Their lives invite us to look past the headlines and statistics, and really see the people who are so often overlooked. They challenge us to question the systems that keep inequality in place. And maybe, just maybe, they inspire us to picture a world where everyone gets a fair shot at thriving.
Have you ever thought about the power in simply remembering—about how telling stories that have almost slipped away can change things? By honoring the lives of the Five, we’re also honoring countless others—voices that history nearly forgot.
That’s their true legacy: a reminder to see, to listen, and to never underestimate the impact of compassion.

As we wrap up this journey, I hope you can still picture those foggy London streets—and the women who walked them with courage and quiet strength.
If you've followed their footsteps, you've seen more than just shadows and crime. You've witnessed the daily bravery it takes to survive when the world feels cold and unforgiving, and the gentle kindnesses that can light up even the darkest corners.
The stories you've heard aren't just echoes from the past—they’re reflections of struggles and strengths that still shape lives today.
So, here’s what I hope you’ll carry with you:
Every life holds dignity, no matter how the world chooses to remember it.
Poverty and hardship? They’re shaped by entire systems, not just the choices of individuals.
Sometimes, it’s the small acts of kindness and a sense of community that become lifelines when things get tough.
And the stories we choose to tell—or leave untold—shape how we see history, and each other.
Reclaiming those forgotten voices is a powerful act of justice and compassion.
It’s easy, isn’t it, to let legends drown out real lives? But when you pause to really listen, and look beyond the headlines, you find something lasting: stubborn hope, the resilience that keeps people moving, and the simple truth that every story matters.
The Five remind us that history isn’t just made by the famous or the powerful—it’s shaped by ordinary people whose lives, however overlooked, are filled with meaning.
As you go forward, let their stories inspire you to notice the unseen, honor the forgotten, and keep the work of remembrance and empathy alive in your own world.
After all, every voice counts—and yours can help shape a more compassionate future.
